# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

These are limits of what the supplied text defines, not additional requirements.

- **Shared-operation boundary:** § Shared operations requires coherent shared records during overlapping work, but does not specify a storage technology, lock mechanism, supported host topology or conflict-resolution mechanism; the implementation must state its operating assumptions and verify the shared operation it supports.
- **Refresh scope:** § Updates and follow-up requires refresh when a settings/policy change affects production or routing of records, but does not enumerate the settings, prescribe a fingerprint format or say that routing-only changes require another model call.

# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Yes. I found the following unresolved points across the four source files. Some are **policy ambiguities**; others are **implementation choices the brief leaves open**. These are research questions, not additional requirements.

In [office-policy.md, “Input export format”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:5), the input boundaries leave these questions:

| # | Point | What remains unclear |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Invalid exports | What happens to invalid JSON, invalid UTF-8, or a missing/non-string `message`: a document error, an import error, or rejection before intake? |
| 2 | Export versions and metadata | Must particular `export_version` values be supported, and are the metadata fields mandatory? No export schema is supplied. |
| 3 | “Up to 200 English words” | Is this a guaranteed input assumption or an enforced limit? Behavior for longer or non-English messages is unspecified. |
| 4 | “Filename” as identity | Does identity use the basename including `.json`, or a relative path when files arrive in different directories? Filename collisions are not addressed. |
| 5 | Identifier comparison | How is the message ID compared with the filename: remove `.json`, compare case-sensitively, normalize whitespace? Otherwise even `IT-001` and `IT-001.json` differ literally. |

In [“Extracted facts”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:10) and [snapshot.schema.json](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/snapshot.schema.json), the field meanings and representation leave these questions:

| # | Point | What remains unclear |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | `request_date` | Is it always the submission date, and which date wins when a message explicitly distinguishes drafting, submission and request dates? |
| 7 | `kind: other` versus `null` | Does `other` mean a clearly unrelated message while `null` means an uncertain classification? That distinction is not defined. |
| 8 | Classification language | How should new/change/withdrawal be recognized when the message uses different wording or never explicitly names its kind? |
| 9 | Normalization | Must names, teams, systems and IDs preserve source spelling/case, or may they be normalized? Which synonyms map to enum values? |
| 10 | Unsupported values | How should explicit environments or permissions outside the enums be represented? The schema excludes them, but the policy gives no specific mapping procedure. |
| 11 | `business_purpose` | Should this be a verbatim passage, a concise summary, or a normalized statement? How much supporting context belongs in it? |
| 12 | “Explicitly labelled as a correction” | Must the word “Correction” appear, or do phrases such as “actually,” “I meant,” and “replace the earlier dates” qualify? |
| 13 | Correction scope | How are partial corrections, corrections to corrections, or multiple incompatible corrections resolved? |
| 14 | “Conflicting” facts | What distinguishes a contradiction from background context, a conditional alternative, or information about someone other than the requester? |
| 15 | Multiple requests in one message | The schema permits one scalar value per field, but no rule addresses a message legitimately requesting several systems, people or access windows. |
| 16 | Date interpretation and validity | How should partial dates, ambiguous numeric dates, invalid calendar dates or timestamps be handled? The schema only requires string/null; the policy adds YYYY-MM-DD. |
| 17 | Empty values and placeholders | Do `""`, whitespace, “unknown,” and “TBD” count as absent values requiring null? The schema permits empty strings, but the policy does not define them. |
| 18 | Supporting quotes and issues | Must every populated fact have evidence, or only selected facts? Are empty evidence arrays allowed? Must issues be separate per fact, and do wording, order or duplicates matter? |

In [“Review queue”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:17), these policy boundaries remain:

| # | Point | What remains unclear |
|---|---|---|
| 19 | “Instruction-override attempt” | What qualifies beyond the obvious supplied example—for instance, quoted instructions, indirect requests to bypass review, or ordinary discussion of approval rules? |
| 20 | Incomplete withdrawal | Rule 2 requires request ID and date, but rule 3 lists required facts only for new/change requests; the fallback for a withdrawal missing either is not fully explicit. |
| 21 | “With request_id and request_date” | Does “with” require non-null, non-empty, semantically valid values, rather than merely schema-valid strings? |
| 22 | “Conflicting details” | Does clarification apply to any contradiction in the narrative, or only contradictions affecting extracted request facts? |
| 23 | “Complete” and `issues` | Is completeness determined strictly by required facts and listed problems, or can any issue prevent normal routing? Informational issues are not classified separately. |
| 24 | Reviewer identity and queue order | The policy names routing groups, but does not map systems to actual human owners or define queue sorting/prioritization. Rule evaluation order does not establish display order. |

The operational terms in [requirements.md, “Operating context”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:7), [“Record and review behavior”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:33), and [policy, “Processing and recovery”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:28) leave these choices:

| # | Point | What remains unclear |
|---|---|---|
| 25 | Workload targets | The text gives ordinary and surge volumes, but no processing deadline, throughput target, memory limit or cost limit. |
| 26 | “Slow” and “available” | No latency threshold is defined, nor precisely how much other processing must progress while one model response remains pending. |
| 27 | Shared-operation boundary | Must overlapping operators be supported on one machine, multiple processes, multiple machines, or all of these? |
| 28 | Duplicate concurrent work | Must overlapping intake avoid duplicate model calls, or only avoid conflicting/duplicate current records? |
| 29 | “Latest processed source” | Is latest determined by intake order, export timestamp, processing start, or completion? The text does not settle out-of-order completion of revisions. |
| 30 | “Coherent” and “agreeing” records | Must queue/extraction agreement hold for every concurrent read and interruption point, or only after an operation completes? |
| 31 | Pending-state representation | How are queued, running and interrupted attempts represented, and what happens to an earlier current result while its replacement is pending? |
| 32 | Interruption recovery boundary | How are abandoned attempts detected, and what happens if a model response arrives just before the application stops but before it records completion? |
| 33 | Retry strategy | Automatic versus operator-triggered retries, retryable errors, limits, delays and timeout values are unspecified. |
| 34 | Reuse after failure | Does an unchanged rerun reuse a recorded failure or retry extraction? How does an explicit retry override reuse after a previous success? |
| 35 | “Reproducible retry command” | Must retry reproduce the original bytes/settings, or process the document’s latest contents using current settings? |
| 36 | “Relevant processing settings” | Which changes invalidate results: provider/model, prompt, schema, sampling parameters, parser, application code or other configuration? |
| 37 | Policy refresh | Does a routing-only policy change reroute existing valid extractions, re-extract messages, or permit either approach? |
| 38 | Provenance and history | What identifies attempts/settings/policy versions, where is history stored, and does history include every failed attempt, raw responses, or only result versions? No retention period is specified. |
| 39 | “Actionable error” and redacted logs | Which diagnostic fields must be recorded, and what logging format and credential-redaction scope are sufficient? |

The provider and submission requirements in [CHALLENGE.md, “What to submit”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/CHALLENGE.md:8) and [requirements.md](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:39) leave these details open:

| # | Point | What remains unclear |
|---|---|---|
| 40 | Supported provider configuration | No provider, model, API endpoint, protocol or runtime is selected; these are implementation choices to document. |
| 41 | “Configurable” settings | Which settings must operators be able to change, and through environment variables, configuration files or command arguments? Only `API_KEY` is prescribed. |
| 42 | Response completion and refusal | Their concrete indicators depend on the selected provider; the supplied files define no provider response contract. |
| 43 | Semantic validation failures | When schema-valid output contains unsupported quotes, inconsistent dates or other semantic defects, should it become an extraction error or a valid extraction requiring clarification? |
| 44 | Extraction wrapper format | No schema defines wrapper field types, the structure of `error`, or the exact provider/model representation of `response_source`. |
| 45 | Queue format | `queue.json` has no supplied schema: array versus object, additional fields, pending entries and provenance representation are unspecified. |
| 46 | Request evidence | How should a JSON file demonstrate “implemented response handling”: descriptive fields, examples, source references or another representation? Must the example be captured or may it be constructed? |
| 47 | Dependency lockfile | No lockfile format is prescribed, and no exception is stated for an application using only standard-library dependencies. |
| 48 | Session capture | The capture format, storage and pairing procedure depend on facilitator instructions outside these four files. |

Finally, [requirements.md, “Verification”](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:41) and [the accuracy deliverable](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/CHALLENGE.md:17) leave these measurement questions:

| # | Point | What remains unclear |
|---|---|---|
| 49 | Scored fields | Does accuracy cover only business facts, or also quotes, issues, routing and wrapper metadata? |
| 50 | Counting and denominator | Are scores per field or per message? How do expected nulls, failed extractions, missing outputs and the synthetic request enter the denominator? |
| 51 | “Exact match” | Are case, whitespace, punctuation, equivalent purpose wording and array order normalized before comparison? |
| 52 | “Factual error” | Does this include omissions, invented facts, wrong classifications and routing errors, or are these reported separately? |
| 53 | Independent expected results | Independence from measured outputs is required, but the authoring/review method and evidence format for expectations are not prescribed. |
| 54 | Paraphrase scope | Which message should be paraphrased, how much wording must change, and which policy cases must the paraphrase exercise? |
| 55 | Mocked accuracy observations | What should be reported as pipeline verification versus model extraction accuracy when mocked responses are used? No minimum accuracy threshold is stated. |
| 56 | Verification depth | The required cases are listed, but repetition counts, operational test scale and interruption points are not; “refusal **or** interrupted responses” also leaves test coverage less explicit than the earlier requirement to handle both. |

Several apparent ambiguities **are already resolved by the text**:

- Rule precedence is explicit: for example, a qualifying withdrawal reaches rule 2 before the identifier-mismatch condition in rule 3.
- Hashes use original file bytes; supporting quotes use decoded message substrings.
- Relative dates remain unresolved; an export timestamp does not supply missing request facts.
- Missing documents in a later batch are not withdrawals.
- Human approval is outside intake decisions.
- Committed deliverables may use mocked or provider responses; a live run is optional.

Several apparent ambiguities **are already resolved by the text**:

- Rule precedence is explicit: for example, a qualifying withdrawal reaches rule 2 before the identifier-mismatch condition in rule 3.
- Hashes use original file bytes; supporting quotes use decoded message substrings.
- Relative dates remain unresolved; an export timestamp does not supply missing request facts.
- Missing documents in a later batch are not withdrawals.
- Human approval is outside intake decisions.
- Committed deliverables may use mocked or provider responses; a live run is optional.
